subject: Copywriting
title: Ogilvy's Long Copy
description: A quick, practical guide to Ogilvy's Long Copy.

hook.text: David Ogilvy believed long copy sold better than short. His Rolls-Royce ad had 607 words and sold out cars.

buildup.text: The headline: 'At 60 mph, the loudest noise comes from the electric clock.' Specific, factual, memorable.

discovery.text: Ogilvy's rule: every word must earn its place. Long copy isn't padding—it's more reasons to believe.

twist.text: Modern marketers say nobody reads long copy. Amazon product pages disagree. So do successful landing pages.

climax.text: Ogilvy proved that people read what interests them. Length matters less than relevance.

punchline.text: 607 words. Sold every car. Long copy isn't dead—boring copy is.

quiz.question: What was Ogilvy's famous Rolls-Royce headline about?

details.summary: David Ogilvy championed research-driven long-form copy, arguing that people who are interested in a product will read every word. His Rolls-Royce ad contained 607 words and became one of the most successful ads in history. Ogilvy proved that long copy sells when it is factual, specific, and...
details.whyItMatters: In an era that fetishizes brevity, Ogilvy's long-copy legacy reminds us that length should serve the reader's need for information. The right length is whatever it takes to persuade.
takeaways: Ogilvy's Rolls-Royce ad used 607 words and produced record sales
Interested readers will read every word of well-written long copy
Long copy outperformed short copy consistently in Ogilvy's tests

faq.question: When does long copy outperform short copy?
faq.answer: For high-consideration purchases, complex products, and audiences seeking information before buying. Long copy also outperforms in direct-response contexts where the ad must do the entire selling job. The key is that every sentence must add value.

faq.question: Is long copy dead in the digital age?
faq.answer: No — long-form landing pages, sales emails, and blog posts continue to convert well. The format has shifted from print to digital, but the principle holds. Long copy works when the reader is motivated and the writing is compelling.
